First it's not 12 years. The US model is 4 of undergrad, 4 of medical school. Then residency is 3 years or more. The primary care residencies are all 3 years. In addition, you can get a license to practice independently after 1 year of residency (though almost all do a full residency). In addition, when you are a resident, you are actually contributing significantly to patient care (and for barely more than minimum wage when I was a resident - a bargain). The UK model is 6 years of school out of high school (instead of 4 + 4) then training to be a GP is generally 2 years, more to be a registrar (specialist). There are also a very few US schools who take exceptional people without a bachelors or who do a 6 year combined program to get a BS and an MD simultaneously. So the range for a primary care physician is 8 years for someone following the UK system and 9-11 the American.

However, the absolute minimum I think is 8 years. You could skip the bachelors and take highly qualified people starting after 2 good years in undergrad, though I think many need 3 or the full 4 years to be prepared for medical school. If you were going to train people exclusively from the get go for only primary care, I think you could get away with 3 years of medical school. However the vast majority of med students don't know if they want primary care when the enter school, so I think that keeping med school proper at 4 years would be best (with perhaps a few schools doing 3 year programs that would only qualify you for certain primary care residency spots.)

I also think that some primary care residents are ready for independent practice after 2 years, though many would need 3 and a few even 4. What would be nice is if residencies could graduate residents when each as an individual is judged to be ready. That is, set a minimum of 2 years, but once a resident is solidly able to work independently, they could be approved, take their boards and if they pass become board certified. This is I think the biggest problem with medical education in the US - it's basically a 1 size fits all program that doesn't take into consideration the significant variance in people's talents and abilities.
